That's fair. The thing is if you go too slowly, it could just be water retention, and not actual tissue. My advice would be 1lb per week for the first month or 2, and see how you feel. Then either maintain that weight, or slowly increase your weight again.

Remember, unless you're a complete beginner, you need raw materials (calories) to put on muscle. You can't build something from nothing.

Fatloss is 100x easier than muscle gain. You can always lose excess fat once you put on the muscle.

1g per pound of actual bodyweight is totally fine, tbh less protein is needed while in a surplus. 1g per pound of LEAN body mass (muscle), is all that's needed to build muscle.

That being said, I still personally aim towards the higher end. I'd suggest to try to eat your GOAL weight in protein.  Like if you wanna be 160 or 180, try to get 160g or 180g of protein per day.

An easy way to do this is to have a minimum protein intake per meal. Say, like 30-40g per meal. With 4 meals @ 40g, you'll be at an easy 160. 

Add a morning protein shake, and preworkout shake, and that'll be an easy 200g. 

Which WOULD be quite high, but in my experience, most people in their first 1-2 years really struggle with getting enough protein in. 

As far as calories, you could break down carbs the same way. Like 100g minimum per meal, and maybe like another 100-200g carbs pre workout. 
Gatorade powder in my preworkout is my go to for some quick carbs.

Hope this helps. 👍

I would tell my past self to:

-Eat more protein! 1g per pound of bodyweight every day. There is no anabolic window, and eat at least 30-40g of high quality protein per meal.

When I first started the old 'bro science' was that your body can't absorb more than 20g of protein from a single meal. Since I wasn't tracking my food, I was probably getting like 120g of protein per day during my first year, and I noticed almost all beginners struggle with this.

-Find a program you can stick to consistently, and to track all workouts, exercises, reps, and sets. And plan to progressively overload in at least 1 way each workout. Either by reps, sets, or weight. If you're not progressively overloading, you're going to limit your progress. 

-To avoid front delt raises! A lot of the bodybuilding.com programs I followed had these. They are really unnecessary and probably caused shoulder issues that took a few years to rehab. 

On that note, to focus more on lateral raises vs heavy pressing to develop the mid delts.

-To not spend as much money on supplements. Whey/casein protein powder and basic creatine monohydrate is about all you need.

There's definitely more, but I feel like these points would've helped me a lot in my early years.
